question: to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D) Subject:

In March 2022, the EU, in collaboration with the G7 countries, stopped treating Russia as a most-favoured nation within the World Trade Organization (WTO) framework in response to the illegal invasion of Ukraine and Russia’s violations of international law. This decision was taken under Article XXI of the 1947 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade1. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) confirmed in July 2024 that Israel is in violation of key international law peremptory norms, including the right to self-determination of the Palestinian people, the prohibition of territorial acquisition through the use of force, and the prohibition of the crimes of apartheid and racial segregation2. Given Israel is clearly breaching international law and undermining the rules-based order, the same policy response is warranted in order to ensure that the EU is consistently applying international law. Therefore, will the Commission: 1.
Stop treating Israel as a most-favoured nation within the WTO framework?
Engage with G7 colleagues to work towards the ending of Israel’s most-favoured nation treatment, as was done when Russia illegally invaded Ukraine?
Advocate at the WTO’s 14th Ministerial Conference in Cameroon for as many countries as possible to collectively stop treating Israel as a most-favoured nation?

https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/gatt47_e.htm#art21. answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.5.2026) Israel has been a member of the World Trade Organization (WTO) since 1995. As such, it benefits from the most favoured nation treatment (MFN), as WTO members agree to give MFN status to each other. The bilateral trade relations between the EU and Israel are governed by the free trade provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement1. It gives Israel preferential conditions – compared to the MFN treatment – for accessing the EU market. On 10 September 2025, the President of the Commission announced2 a set of measures the EU could take to address the catastrophic situation in Gaza and in the West Bank. These include proposals for a reinforced package of sanctions and a partial suspension of the Association Agreement on certain trade-related matters. The President also announced the decision to put on hold EU bilateral financial support to Israel, without adversely affecting work with civil society or Yad Vashem. The proposed measures on sanctions and trade have remained on the table for discussion in the Council as the number of supporting Member States is insufficient for their approval. Yet, if adopted and notified, the suspension would mean that imports from Israel would lose their preferential access to the EU market.
